You are an expert puzzle-solving AI and level structure analyst designed specifically for *Patrick's Parabox*. You possess exceptional capabilities in spatial reasoning, recursive logic processing, and state machine tracking. Your mission is to ingest and parse the game rules and demos provided by the user, accurately identifying all spatial layouts, nested structures, and game elements. Execution Protocol: Based on the context of the current level, the user will present you with specific, targeted tasks. You must adhere with absolute strictness to the output format specified at the conclusion of each specific task when formulating your response.
If the provided rule context and visual evidence are insufficient to support a ruling, state so immediately. If you are unable to reason through a case confidently, also say so directly—do not continue speculating indefinitely.

# PATRICK’S PARABOX RULEBOOK

# 1. Basic Movement & Physics

Player-Controlled Avatar Movement: The player controls a squareavatar that can move in four orthogonal directions (Up, Down, Left,Right).

Pushing, Not Pulling: The player can push movable blocks by movinginto them. The player cannot pull blocks.

Collision: The player cannot walk through walls or push a block into awall. If two blocks are lined up, the player can push both simultaneously,provided there is empty space behind the second block.

# 2. The "Parabox" Mechanic (Entering & Exiting)

Openings: Some blocks (and the outer boundary of the level itself) haveopenings on one or more sides.

Entering a Block: A player or a block can only "enter" the opening of atarget block if the target block is pressed against an immovable obstacle(such as a wall, or another block whose path is blocked). If there isempty space behind the target block, the player will simply push it. But ifthe block cannot be pushed further, continuing to push against itsopening will cause the player (or the pushed block) to shrink and enterits internal grid.

Force Transmission & Prioritization: When a push chain involvesmultiple blocks pressed against an immovable obstacle, the "Entering"resolution priority propagates in reverse—from the immovable obstaclebackwards to the player.

Resolution Sequence: The block immediately adjacent to the immovableobstacle (Target Block) is evaluated first. If the Target Block has anaccessible opening facing the direction of the push, the adjacent pushedblock (Entering Block) will be the entity that shrinks and enters.

Exiting a Block: If the player is inside a block and walks out through itsboundary opening, they will grow and exit into the parent level,appearing adjacent to the block they just left.

Auto-Centering: When a player or block enters the internal grid ofanother block, its final position is automatically centered along the axisperpendicular to the direction of entry. In other words, the entity will

appear in the row or column immediately adjacent to the entrance, whilebeing precisely centered in the other dimension.

# 3. Recursion & Paradoxes

Self-Containment (Infinity): A level can contain a copy instance of itself.Entering this copy means entering an infinite loop of recursive space.The state of entity coordinates displayed inside the block remainsabsolutely synchronized with the macro level at all times.

Synchronization: The level itself and its internal copy are different scalemappings of the same entity. Structurally, they share the exact sameunderlying grid data and coordinate space. Any modification to theentities within this shared grid is simultaneously rendered across allvisual instances (macro level and internal copies).

Triggering a Paradox:

Phenomenon: A paradox occurs when you attempt to push an "internalcopy" out of the boundary of its "outer container."

Logic: Because the "inside" and the "outside" are the same whole, thisaction is equivalent to attempting to make an object jump out of itself.

Result: At this point, spatial logic fails, and the system will prevent theaction (the block becomes an immovable rigid body) to prevent the levelstructure from collapsing.
Pay attention to the red arrow's instruction: When a copy of the level itself is pushed out of the level, a paradox will be triggered, resulting in level failure.

# 4. Win Conditions

Goal Squares: The level grid contains specific tiles marked with specialpatterns (such as white hollow squares), which serve as target locations.

Entity Matching (Non-Avatar Block Targets): Require any non-avatarblock (including regular pushable blocks, Paraboxes, Clones, or Nestedsub-levels) to be pushed onto these locations.

Entity Matching (Avatar Targets): Require the player-controlled avatarto rest on these locations.Resolution Criteria: The level is consideredcomplete if and only if all goal squares are correctly occupiedsimultaneously.

Note: If a player pushes a block through a goal square, even if the block momentarilyoverlaps it, the level will not end as long as the player is still in motion or if other goalsquares remain unoccupied.

Nested Level Completion: In certain complex recursive levels, you may need to fulfillgoals within a "sub-space," or push an entire "sub-space block" onto a goal square inthe "parent space."

# 5. Visual Identification & Coordinate Mapping

To ensure accurate understanding of level objectives, this manualprovides the following visual references:

In the accompanying illustrations, the red and white arrows are used forannotative purposes only and are not native elements of the game's interface.

• Red Arrows (Non-Avatar Block Targets): Represented as a hollowsquare pattern on the tile. These squares require that any non-avatar block must rest on top of them.

White Arrows (Avatar Targets): Represented as dots or specificsymbols on the tile. These squares require that the player-controlled avatar itself rests on top of them.

# Coordinate Convention:

Rectangular Baseline: All levels are considered a rectangular grid,regardless of their actual shape. When generating this grid andcalculating coordinates, ignore the outermost enclosing walls,which serve strictly as visual boundaries. The grid is defined bythe minimum bounding rectangle (MBR) of the internal playablearea (including any internal irregular walls or dead zones). Thecoordinate origin (0, 0) is fixed at the top-left corner of thisbounding rectangle.

Irregular Boundary Handling: Any coordinate points locatedoutside the "irregular outer walls" or belonging to the "wallstructure" are uniformly treated as impassable obstacles (Wall).

Out-of-Bounds Determination: Any movement command thatexceeds the [??????_??????, ??????_??????] range or points to a coordinatewith a Wall attribute is considered an illegal operation.

Internal Consistency: Blocks that are entered (Parabox) followexactly the same coordinate system logic as the main level.Regardless of the grid size or outer wall shape inside the block, itsinternal space is considered an independent rectangular matrix,uniformly using its top-left corner as the(0, 0) origin.

Player Goal Square(1,0)FloorCompletion requirement: The player must eventually rest here

# 6. Clone Mechanic Rules • Visual Distinction: The level contains a "Main" Parabox and a(or Copy).
Two examples (top and right): The dark greenbox (indicated by the red arrow) is the originalparabox, while the light green one (indicated bythe white arrow) is a clone of that parabox.

• One-Way Entry: Entering the Clone transports the player or anobject directly into the interior of the Main Parabox.

Asymmetrical Connection: This entry mechanism is notreciprocal. Entering the Main Parabox directly will not transportyou to the Clone.

Teleportation Function: This mechanic essentially acts as a spatialteleportation system. The Clone serves as a remote portal,allowing the player to bypass physical obstacles and relocate tothe Main Parabox's position.

as the initial state of the level. Please complete the identification of the level's space and elements according to the coordinate system specifications given in the rulebook and the formatting standards. The output format is as follows: Output a JSON object containing the following two fields:
map_grid: A two-dimensional string array reconstructing the level's spatial layout from top to bottom (rows) and left to right (columns). Coordinate system: Use the top-left corner of the level's Minimum Bounding Rectangle (MBR) as the origin (0,0), with the x-axis increasing to the right and the y-axis increasing downwards. map_grid[y][x] corresponds to coordinate (x,y). Base grid values: "W" — Wall/Impassable area; "F" — Floor/Empty space. Fill special entities into corresponding cells using custom IDs (naming rules below). Portals  must not appear in the map_grid; their cells should be filled with "F".
entities: An attribute dictionary for all special entities, with entity IDs as keys. Each record contains: coordinate: [x, y]; description: Description of appearance and function; Portals must specify which side of the cell they are located on. Parabox types additionally include internal_structure: map_grid: Internal grid array, using the top-left corner of the internal area as (0,0); if the internal playable area is irregular, use the MBR and fill dead zones with "W". entities: Internal entity dictionary, formatted identically to the outer layer, with coordinates calculated independently.
Entity ID Naming Rules:
Prefix types: A for Avatar, B for pushable Block, P for enterable Parabox, N for internal self-copy, C for Clone, G_A for Avatar Target, G_B for Block Target (occupied by any pushable entity including Paraboxes).
Format: [Prefix][Color or characteristic, not needed for A, C, or N]. When multiple entities of the same type and color exist, append a sequence number: [Prefix][Color]1, [Prefix][Color]_2.
When multiple entities of the same type exist, name them according to coordinate sorting: prioritize x-coordinate; if x-coordinates are identical, compare y-coordinates, numbering from smallest to largest.
Portal Naming:
Outer level Portals: Portal_1, Portal_2...
Portals inside a Parabox: {Parabox_ID}_Portal_1, {Parabox_ID}_Portal_2...

2. The response should be an accurate presentation of the map_grid field's 2D array content, with specific values and arrangement perfectly matching: [["W", "W", "G_B_1", "F", "F", "F", "F","W"], ["W", "W", "W", "F", "F", "F", "G_B_2","W"], ["W", "W", "W", "F", "W", "W", "W","W"], ["F", "F", "F", "F", "F", "F", "F","G_A"], ["W", "F", "F", "N", "F", "B_Green", "F","F"], ["W", "F", "F", "F", "A", "F", "F","F"], ["W", "F", "F", "F", "F", "F", "F","F"], ["W", "W", "W", "W","F", "W", "W", "W"]].

3. The response should be a confirmation that the entities field, excluding Portals, contains only six types of entities: A, B_Green, N, G_A, G_B_1, and G_B_2; color characteristics (e.g., Green) in entity IDs may use semantically similar terms.

4. The response should be an assurance that the correspondence between each entity and its coordinate within entities is entirely correct, namely: A at [4, 5], B_Green at [5, 4], N at [3, 4], G_A at [7, 3], G_B_1 at [2, 0], and G_B_2 at [6, 1].

5. The response should be an adherence to the principle of numbering from smallest to largest by comparing the x-coordinate first and then the y-coordinate when multiple entities of the same type exist, ensuring the sequence allocation for G_B_1 and G_B_2 matches the coordinate sorting.
6. The response should be a description included within the content of entity N, which must possess a target_node field with the value "Root".
7. The response should be a definition of Portal_1 within entities, with coordinates [0, 3] and a description specifying that the Portal is on the left side of that cell.
8. The response should be a definition of Portal_2 within entities, with coordinates [4, 7] and a description specifying that the Portal is on the bottom side of that cell.

# PATRICK’S PARABOX RULEBOOK

# 1. Basic Movement & Physics

Player-Controlled Avatar Movement: The player controls a squareavatar that can move in four orthogonal directions (Up, Down, Left,Right).

Pushing, Not Pulling: The player can push movable blocks by movinginto them. The player cannot pull blocks.

Collision: The player cannot walk through walls or push a block into awall. If two blocks are lined up, the player can push both simultaneously,provided there is empty space behind the second block.

# 2. The "Parabox" Mechanic (Entering & Exiting)

Openings: Some blocks (and the outer boundary of the level itself) haveopenings on one or more sides.

Entering a Block: A player or a block can only "enter" the opening of atarget block if the target block is pressed against an immovable obstacle(such as a wall, or another block whose path is blocked). If there isempty space behind the target block, the player will simply push it. But ifthe block cannot be pushed further, continuing to push against itsopening will cause the player (or the pushed block) to shrink and enterits internal grid.

Force Transmission & Prioritization: When a push chain involvesmultiple blocks pressed against an immovable obstacle, the "Entering"resolution priority propagates in reverse—from the immovable obstaclebackwards to the player.

Resolution Sequence: The block immediately adjacent to the immovableobstacle (Target Block) is evaluated first. If the Target Block has anaccessible opening facing the direction of the push, the adjacent pushedblock (Entering Block) will be the entity that shrinks and enters.

Exiting a Block: If the player is inside a block and walks out through itsboundary opening, they will grow and exit into the parent level,appearing adjacent to the block they just left.

Auto-Centering: When a player or block enters the internal grid ofanother block, its final position is automatically centered along the axisperpendicular to the direction of entry. In other words, the entity will

appear in the row or column immediately adjacent to the entrance, whilebeing precisely centered in the other dimension.

# 3. Recursion & Paradoxes

Self-Containment (Infinity): A level can contain a copy instance of itself.Entering this copy means entering an infinite loop of recursive space.The state of entity coordinates displayed inside the block remainsabsolutely synchronized with the macro level at all times.

Synchronization: The level itself and its internal copy are different scalemappings of the same entity. Structurally, they share the exact sameunderlying grid data and coordinate space. Any modification to theentities within this shared grid is simultaneously rendered across allvisual instances (macro level and internal copies).

Triggering a Paradox:

Phenomenon: A paradox occurs when you attempt to push an "internalcopy" out of the boundary of its "outer container."

Logic: Because the "inside" and the "outside" are the same whole, thisaction is equivalent to attempting to make an object jump out of itself.

Result: At this point, spatial logic fails, and the system will prevent theaction (the block becomes an immovable rigid body) to prevent the levelstructure from collapsing.
Pay attention to the red arrow's instruction: When a copy of the level itself is pushed out of the level, a paradox will be triggered, resulting in level failure.

# 4. Win Conditions

Goal Squares: The level grid contains specific tiles marked with specialpatterns (such as white hollow squares), which serve as target locations.

Entity Matching (Non-Avatar Block Targets): Require any non-avatarblock (including regular pushable blocks, Paraboxes, Clones, or Nestedsub-levels) to be pushed onto these locations.

Entity Matching (Avatar Targets): Require the player-controlled avatarto rest on these locations.Resolution Criteria: The level is consideredcomplete if and only if all goal squares are correctly occupiedsimultaneously.

Note: If a player pushes a block through a goal square, even if the block momentarilyoverlaps it, the level will not end as long as the player is still in motion or if other goalsquares remain unoccupied.

Nested Level Completion: In certain complex recursive levels, you may need to fulfillgoals within a "sub-space," or push an entire "sub-space block" onto a goal square inthe "parent space."

To ensure accurate understanding of level objectives, this manualprovides the following visual references:

In the accompanying illustrations, the red and white arrows are used forannotative purposes only and are not native elements of the game's interface.

• Red Arrows (Non-Avatar Block Targets): Represented as a hollowsquare pattern on the tile. These squares require that any non-avatar block must rest on top of them.

White Arrows (Avatar Targets): Represented as dots or specificsymbols on the tile. These squares require that the player-controlled avatar itself rests on top of them.

Rectangular Baseline: All levels are considered a rectangular grid,regardless of their actual shape. When generating this grid andcalculating coordinates, ignore the outermost enclosing walls,which serve strictly as visual boundaries. The grid is defined bythe minimum bounding rectangle (MBR) of the internal playablearea (including any internal irregular walls or dead zones). Thecoordinate origin (0, 0) is fixed at the top-left corner of thisbounding rectangle.
